title: From source to program
objectives: Compile and run a C++ program from the terminal, and read a compiler error.

screens.title: Two commands, not one
screens.prose: In Python you run the source file itself: `python3 main.py`. Here is a C++ session in a terminal. The folder starts with one file, `main.cpp`, the text of the program.
screens.question: Tap the command that turns `main.cpp` into a program the machine can run.

hints.text: Which command makes a new file appear in the folder?
Compare the two `ls` listings, before and after.
The file `main` appears after line 3, so line 3 made it.

feedback.correct: `g++` read the text and wrote a new file, `main`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the command that changes what `ls` lists.

byKey.l6: You tapped the command that runs the program. By then `main` already existed: the `ls` on line 4 shows it.
byKey.l7: That is the program's output. Something had to build the program before it could print.
byKey.l1: `ls` only lists the folder. Compare its two listings to see what changed between them.
byKey.l4: `ls` only lists the folder. The command before it is the one that made `main`.

explain.text: `g++` is a **compiler**. It read `main.cpp` and wrote `main`, a file of machine instructions. `./main` runs that file directly, and nothing reads `main.cpp` again.

screens.prose: Inside that one `g++` command are two steps, drawn here. The program uses `std::cout` to print, yet you never wrote the code that prints. That code was compiled long ago and sits in a library.
screens.question: Tap the step where the library's printing code joins your code.

hints.text: Follow the arrow that leaves the library box.
The library's arrow ends at one step.

feedback.correct: The linker joins `main.o` and the library into one file.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrow out of the library box.

byKey.cc: The compiler sees only your file. `#include <iostream>` tells it `std::cout` exists, but the printing code itself is not there.
byKey.lib: That box holds the printing code, but it does nothing by itself. Find the step its arrow points to.
byKey.exe: That is the finished program, after the join.
byKey.obj: `main.o` is your code alone, with a gap where `std::cout` goes.

explain.text: The **compiler** turns `main.cpp` into an **object file**, `main.o`: machine code with gaps for names defined elsewhere. The **linker** fills the gaps from the library and writes the **executable**, `main`. `g++ main.cpp -o main` runs both and deletes `main.o` afterwards.

screens.title: Editing without rebuilding
screens.prose: So the **compiler** makes an **object file** and the **linker** makes the **executable**. Python reads `main.py` afresh on every run. Now you change `"Hello, market"` to `"Hello, desk"` in `main.cpp` and save it.
screens.question: You type `./main` without running `g++` again. What prints?

options.why: You expected `./main` to read `main.cpp`, as `python3` reads `main.py`. The executable was built before the edit and never looks at the source.

options.text: An error saying the source has changed
options.why: Nothing checks the source when `./main` runs. The old executable runs as it always did.
Saving changes only `main.cpp`. The executable stays exactly as it was.

hints.text: Which box does `./main` run?
The edit changed this box only.
`main` was built from the old text. Nothing has rebuilt it.

feedback.correct: The executable still holds the old text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which file `./main` actually runs.

byKey.new: You expected `./main` to read `main.cpp`, as `python3` reads `main.py`. It runs the executable, which was built before your edit.

explain.text: `./main` runs the executable, which was built from the old text. The edit reaches it only when you compile again. After every edit, run `g++` before `./main`.

screens.title: Your first program
screens.prose: Every C++ program starts in `int main()`. `#include <iostream>` brings in `std::cout`, and `<<` sends text to it. `'\n'` ends the line, and every statement ends with `;`. Here Check does the `g++` step for you: the compiler runs inside your browser.
screens.question: Write the program that prints `Hello, market` on its own line.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and can take up to a minute; later Checks take a few seconds. Check compiles your program and runs it 3 times. One run compares the output character for character, so end the line with '\n'.

hints.text: Start the line with `std::cout <<`.
The text goes in double quotes; the line end is `'\n'`.
`std::cout << "Hello, market" << '\n';` inside `main`, before `return 0;`.

feedback.correct: That is a complete C++ program.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your output with the expected line under the editor.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Read the first `error:` line under the editor: it names the line and the column.
byKey.test-2: The words match but not every character. Check the comma, the capital H and the `'\n'` at the end.

explain.text:
`std::cout` is the screen, and `<<` pushes each piece onto it in order. `return 0;` tells the shell the program succeeded.

```cpp
std::cout << "Hello, market" << '\n';
```

screens.title: Reading input
screens.prose: `std::cin >> x` reads the next word typed into `x`, skipping spaces and line breaks. Unlike Python's `input()`, it converts to the type of `x` for you, so a `double` reads a number.

state.caption: You type lines 2 and 3; the program prints lines 4 and 5.

screens.question: Read a ticker and a price with `std::cin`, then print them on two lines as shown.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and can take up to a minute; later Checks take a few seconds. Check runs your program 4 times, each with different input on std::cin, and compares what it prints.

hints.text: One `std::cin` line can read both: `std::cin >> ticker >> price;`.
Test 2 types both on one line. `>>` skips the space for you.
Then two `std::cout` lines, each ending with `'\n'`.

feedback.correct: `>>` read a word, then a number, and converted it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the first failing test's output with the expected lines.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 types `BARC 215.35` on one line. `std::cin >>` stops at the space, so read twice with `>>`, not a whole line.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 expects `12000`. Leave the number as `std::cout` prints it; do not fix the decimal places.

explain.text: `std::cin >> ticker >> price;` reads a word into the `std::string`, then converts the next word into the `double`. Spaces and line breaks between them make no difference.

screens.title: Reading a compiler error
screens.prose: You forget a semicolon and build. g++ prints an error in the shape `file:line:column: error: message`.
screens.question: Tap the line of `main.cpp` that the error names.

hints.text: Read the number straight after `main.cpp:` in the error line.
That error line is marked red.
`main.cpp:5:5` means line 5, column 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first number after `main.cpp:`.

byKey.l4: That is where the slip is, and we come to it next. The error itself names line 5: read the number after `main.cpp:`.
byKey.l6: The error names line 5. Read the first number after `main.cpp:`.

explain.text: `main.cpp:5:5` is the file, then line 5, then column 5. g++ also prints that line with a caret under the column. So the error is reported at `std::cout` on line 5.

screens.prose: Same error. Line 5 looks perfectly fine, though: it is the same `std::cout` line that worked before.
screens.question: Tap the line you must change to fix the build.

hints.text: The message says what it expected: `','` or `';'`.
Look at how the line above line 5 ends.
`double price = 101.5` never ends, so the compiler read on into line 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the end of the line above the one the error names.

byKey.l5: Line 5 is where g++ noticed, not where the slip is. The declaration on line 4 never ended, so the compiler read straight on into line 5.

explain.text: g++ reports where it got confused, often the line after the slip. Clang, the compiler in this app, points at the end of line 4 instead: `expected ';' at end of declaration`. Either way, read the named line and the one above it.

screens.title: Warnings and a missing return
screens.question: What happened?

options.text: It built and ran: a warning is advice, and `main` returns 0 by itself
It did not build, because of the warning
options.why: You read `warning` as `error`. Only an error stops the build; line 6 shows `./main` running.

options.text: It built, but `main` returns a random exit code
options.why: `main` is the one function where reaching the end returns 0. Any other function that promises a value must `return` one.

options.text: It built only because `-Wall` was given
options.why: `-Wall` asks for more warnings. It never makes a build succeed or fail.

hints.text: Is there an `error:` anywhere in the output?
Line 6 tries to run the program.

feedback.correct: A warning flags something odd; it does not stop the build.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the word `error` and for what line 6 does.

byKey.nobuild: You read `warning` as `error`. Only an error stops the build, and line 6 shows `./main` running.

explain.text: g++ built `main` despite the warning, which only says `qty` is never used. `main` may end without `return 0;` and still report success. Read warnings anyway: they often point at a real bug.

screens.title: A Python habit that compiles
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read `=` as `==`. The test is false, so `flat` is skipped, but `=` still stored 0 in `signals`.
`signals = 0` has the value 0, and 0 counts as false. The body of the `if` never runs.
In Python, `if signals = 0:` is a syntax error. C++ accepts an assignment as a condition, and g++ stays silent without `-Wall`.

hints.text: In C++, `=` always stores a value, even inside `if ( )`.
After `signals = 0`, what does `signals` hold? That is what line 3 shows.
The condition's value is 0, which is false, and `signals` is now 0.

feedback.correct: The `if` stored 0 and then tested it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat `=` as storing, wherever it appears.

byKey.three: You read `=` as `==`. The condition stored 0 in `signals`, so the last line prints 0.
byKey.noc: You expected the Python rule. C++ accepts an assignment as a condition, so this builds and runs.

explain.text: `signals = 0` stores 0 and has the value 0, which is false. The test was meant to be `signals == 0`. Clang warns about this by default and g++ with `-Wall`, which is one reason to read warnings.

screens.prose: Put the life of a C++ program in order, from typing it to the shell hearing it finished.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: The compiler turns it into `main.o`, with gaps for `std::cout`
The linker fills the gaps from the library and writes `main`
`main` returns 0, and the shell reads that as success

hints.text: Nothing can run until the executable exists.
The object file comes before the executable.
Write, compile, link, run, return.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows on the diagram.

explain.text: The diagram is the order: source, compiler, object file, linker, executable. Running comes last, and `main`'s return value is the last thing the shell sees.

screens.title: A long error from a library
screens.prose: Desks write pricers in C++ because compiled loops, such as a binomial tree, often run tens of times faster than plain Python. In a backtest you try to print a whole `std::vector<double>` of closes. g++ prints 232 lines. Here are the first few.

lines: main.cpp:6:15: error: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::ostream' {aka 'std::basic_ostream<char>'} and 'std::vector<double>')
/usr/include/c++/13/ostream:110:36: note:   no known conversion for argument 1 from 'std::vector<double>' to ...
params.title: Terminal

screens.question: Tap the line that says, in words, what went wrong.

hints.text: Skip every line that says `note:`.
Only one line says `error:`.
Read it as: there is no `<<` that takes a stream on the left and a vector on the right.

feedback.correct: No `<<` exists for a stream and a whole vector.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the one line marked `error:` in your own file.

byKey.l6: You picked a `note:`. Notes list every `<<` the compiler tried and rejected; the problem is stated once, in the `error:` line.
byKey.l7: You picked a `note:`. Notes list every `<<` the compiler tried and rejected; the problem is stated once, in the `error:` line.
byKey.l8: You picked a `note:`. The notes only list rejected candidates. Read the `error:` line instead.
byKey.l5: That line says which header the notes come from. The problem itself is in the `error:` line.

explain.text: In words: `std::cout` has no `<<` for a whole `std::vector<double>`, so print the closes one at a time in a loop. The notes list every candidate the compiler tried. Read the first `error:` in your own file and ignore the rest at first.

ideas: A C++ program is built before it runs: the compiler makes an object file and the linker makes the executable.
`./main` runs the executable, so every edit needs a fresh build.
Read `file:line:column: error:`, then check the named line and the one above it. Warnings do not stop a build.

formula.name: Build and run
formula.note: `g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp -o main` does both steps; `./main` runs the result.

summary.trap: `if (x = 0)` compiles: it stores 0 and tests false. Comparison is `==`.

quiz.prose:
```text
main.cpp:5:18: error: 'pirce' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'price'?
    5 |     std::cout << pirce << '\n';
```
quiz.question: What is the fix?

options.text: Declare a new variable `pirce` above line 5
options.why: That silences the error but prints a different, new variable. The message suggests the name you meant.
Headers bring in library names. `pirce` is a misspelling of your own variable.
A missing semicolon gives `expected ';'`. This message says a name is unknown.

feedback.correct: A typo in a name: the compiler even suggests the fix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the end of the message: `did you mean`.

explain.text: "Not declared in this scope" means the compiler has never met that name. Here it is a typo, and the compiler suggests `price`.

options.why: `prices.cpp` is the source text. The machine runs the executable that `-o` named.
`pricer` is machine code, not Python. Run it directly with `./`.
`g++` builds programs; it does not run them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `-o` names the output file.

explain.text: `-o pricer` tells g++ to call the executable `pricer`. `./` means "in this folder", so `./pricer` runs it.

quiz.prose: The program starts with `#include <iostream>` and nothing else above `main`.
quiz.question: Which line, inside `main`, compiles?

options.why: That is Python. C++ has no `print` function here; it uses `std::cout <<`.
Every C++ statement ends with `;`. This one never ends.
`cout` lives inside `std`. Without `std::` the compiler does not know the name.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check for `std::` and a final `;`.

explain.text: C++ needs the full name `std::cout` and a `;` at the end of every statement. `print` is a Python habit.

quiz.prose: A build prints two warnings and no errors.
quiz.question: Is there a new executable?

options.text: Yes: warnings do not stop the build
No: any warning stops the build
options.why: You read warnings as errors. Only an `error:` line stops the build.

options.text: Only an object file, with no executable
options.why: Warnings stop neither step. Both compile and link finish.

options.text: No, the old executable is kept
options.why: With no errors, the linker writes a new executable over the old one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a warning stop?

explain.text: A warning is advice about code that compiles; the build still finishes. An error means there is no new executable at all.
